cues.text: A Martyr Known Almost Entirely by Legend
Although Christopher is among the most popular saints of both East and West, the Catholic Encyclopedia states the matter plainly: almost nothing certain is known about his life or death.
His name, from the Greek Christophoros, means simply "Christ-bearer."
He appears to have been a genuine martyr of the third century, most likely under Emperor Decius’s persecution around 251.
This bare historical kernel was later expanded considerably by centuries of devotion.
The Legend of a Giant's Search
A widely circulated legend, traceable in Greek form perhaps to the sixth century and spread through France by the ninth, tells of a man of enormous size and strength.
Called Offerus, Reprobus, or Adokimus in different versions, he resolved to serve only the greatest king he could find.
Finding first an earthly king and then, by his own account, the devil himself, wanting in courage, he was directed by a hermit to serve Christ instead.
He was instructed to use his great strength ferrying travelers across a dangerous river.
Carrying the Christ Child
Later medieval versions of the legend were gathered in the thirteenth-century Golden Legend.
They relate that one day Offerus carried a small child across the river, growing steadily heavier with every step, until he seemed to bear the whole world’s weight on his shoulders.
The child, the story holds, revealed himself as Christ the Creator and Redeemer, and gave Offerus the new name Christopher — Christ-bearer — in memory of the crossing.
Martyrdom

The Golden Legend and earlier passios place Christopher's death under a persecuting official in Lycia, in Asia Minor, where his preaching is said to have converted many before he was imprisoned, tortured, and finally beheaded.
As with the river-crossing narrative, these details of his trial and death belong to later legendary embellishment rather than to any contemporary record.
The Church's ancient martyrologies do preserve the simple, older memory of a martyr named Christopher honored from a very early date.
Legacy

Devotion to Christopher as patron of travelers spread widely across medieval Christendom, and his image, or a medal bearing his name, remains a familiar sight in vehicles and among pilgrims to this day.
In the 1969 reform of the General Roman Calendar, his feast was removed from the universal calendar because so little could be historically verified about him.
It may still be kept locally, and popular devotion to him has never diminished.
Whatever the precise shape of the man behind the legend, the story the Church has told of him for fifteen centuries carries its own enduring truth.
The humblest labor, offered patiently and without complaint in service of the stranger, can become, unknowingly, a carrying of Christ himself.
